evaluation.positioning_hook: A laid-off Manhattan data analyst turns his suicide into a market-moving spectacle, then tries to outsmart AI, Wall Street, and his own best friend for millions.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The premise is instantly legible and built for conversation: a suicidal layoff victim becomes a financial instrument, and every escalation is easy to pitch in one sentence. The audience is narrower than a four-quadrant crowd because of the dark subject matter and dense finance/tech satire, but the hook is unusually strong.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands immediately in the opening pages with Jesse's layoff, the suicide countdown, and the prediction market mechanic. The script keeps restating the engine through concrete turns—Harvard Club, tour, Nervy, Palm Beach—so the premise never gets muddy.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jesse is vivid because he is both pathetic and strategic, and Mikey/Andrea give the story a relational triangle with real pressure. The characters are strong enough to carry the feature, though Jesse is still more concept-forward than psychologically layered.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script takes a wildly specific satirical swing: AI layoffs, suicide markets, creator platforms, and political power brokers all collide in one escalating machine. The tonal audacity is real, especially in the way it treats public self-destruction as both media event and financial product.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps finding new engines—viral post, corporate panic, market manipulation, live tour, streamer deal, Palm Beach climax—so it rarely sits still. A few stretches lean on dialogue-heavy explanation, but the escalation pattern is strong and the set pieces keep changing shape.

resonant_originality.reasoning: This is one of those rare premises that feels bizarre on first read and obvious in hindsight: a man monetizes the public's certainty about his death. The idea is fresh, but it also maps cleanly onto current anxieties about AI, attention markets, and the commodification of despair.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world is unusually specific: Manhattan nightlife, tech-office culture, prediction markets, creator platforms, Palm Beach power circles, and Miami family life all have distinct texture. The script keeps generating story from institutions and status systems rather than just using them as backdrop.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The voice is sharply satirical, but it also has a sincere undercurrent of grief and class resentment that keeps the comedy from floating away. The tonal identity is distinctive because it can pivot from corporate absurdism to intimate humiliation to political grotesque without losing its center.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: Under the high-concept engine, there are real layers about obsolescence, masculinity, class betrayal, and the monetization of hopelessness. The script hints at more than it fully explores, which gives it depth without quite reaching the level of a truly inexhaustible character study.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jesse, Mikey, and Andrea form a volatile triangle that can generate scenes almost anywhere, and the corporate/power-world supporting cast adds additional friction. The ensemble is not sprawling, but the relationships are active enough that multiple pairings can carry material.

lead_characters.name: Jesse Peterson
lead_characters.demographics: White male, mid-20s, laid-off data analyst, urban professional, likely college-educated.
lead_characters.hook: A smart, self-mythologizing data analyst who turns his layoff into a public death countdown, Jesse is equal parts wounded, vain, funny, and opportunistic. He wants dignity, money, and control in a world that has already decided he is obsolete, and he keeps discovering that his worst impulses are also his best survival tools.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Jesse Eisenberg in The Social Network or Jeremy Strong in Succession: a fast-talking, self-justifying pressure cooker role that lets an actor play humiliation, intelligence, and moral collapse in the same scene.

lead_characters.name: Mikey
lead_characters.demographics: White male, late-20s, Jesse's best friend, employed, in a serious relationship.
lead_characters.hook: Mikey is the grounded friend who keeps getting pulled into Jesse's chaos because loyalty and self-interest are hard to separate. He reads as the moral center until the script reveals how easily he can be seduced by the same money logic he condemns.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Adam Driver in Marriage Story or Paul Dano in The Fabelmans a chance to play restraint under pressure; the appeal is the slow burn of a decent man discovering his own complicity.

lead_characters.name: Andrea
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid-20s, Mikey's girlfriend/fiancée, ambitious, finance-minded, likely Ivy/MBA track.
lead_characters.hook: Andrea is the sharpest strategist in the room, and she understands the market logic of Jesse's crisis faster than anyone else. She is emotionally attached to Mikey but intellectually drawn to the hustle, which makes her both indispensable and dangerous.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that let Sarah Snook in Succession or Jodie Comer in The Last Duel play intelligence as seduction; the showcase is a woman who can weaponize composure while still letting the cracks show.

lead_characters.name: Brenda McMahon
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 30s, COO, corporate executive, polished, high-status professional.
lead_characters.hook: Brenda is the corporate fixer who can speak compassion, legalese, and threat in the same breath. She is one of the few characters who can meet Jesse on his own rhetorical level, which makes her feel like both antagonist and mirror.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong Glenn Close in Damages or Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects territory: a controlled, high-IQ operator role that rewards precision, authority, and the ability to turn warmth into menace.

lead_characters.name: Devin Lee
lead_characters.demographics: Asian male, 40s, CEO, tech founder, physically performative, status-conscious.
lead_characters.hook: Devin is the kind of founder who has internalized the market's cruelty and now performs it back at everyone beneath him. His panic is comic, but the script also lets him register as a man who knows the machine is bigger than him and keeps pretending otherwise.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Ken Watanabe in Godzilla or Steven Yeun in Beef a chance to play authority cracking under absurd pressure; the fun is in the collapse of polish.

lead_characters.name: Mario de Amor
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 40s, wealthy AI founder, elite, cosmopolitan, likely Latin American or Latino-coded by name and setting.
lead_characters.hook: Mario is the script's philosophical villain: a billionaire technologist who treats human suffering as data and moral catastrophe as an experiment. He is articulate, theatrical, and terrifying because he believes he is serving history.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the prestige-villain lift of Michael Stuhlbarg in Dopesick or Giancarlo Esposito in Better Call Saul: elegant menace, ideological certainty, and big monologue territory.

lead_characters.name: Kayla
lead_characters.demographics: Female, 20s, stripper/sex worker, socially agile, financially motivated.
lead_characters.hook: Kayla is more than a temptation figure; she is a hustler who recognizes Jesse's vulnerability and turns it into leverage. She can be tender, transactional, and predatory in the same scene, which keeps her from reading as a simple plot device.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Sydney Sweeney in Reality or Juno Temple in Fargo a chance to play charm with a blade under it; the showcase is volatility plus control.

lead_characters.name: Chase
lead_characters.demographics: Male, 20s, white, aggressive, working-class, later bodyguard role.
lead_characters.hook: Chase starts as a nightclub antagonist and becomes an unlikely follower, which gives him a useful volatility. He is the kind of guy who can be dangerous, pathetic, and loyal depending on who is paying him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is a strong character-actor part in the vein of Joe Cole in Gangs of London or Ben Foster in Hell or High Water: physical menace with a surprising emotional turn.

lead_characters.name: Carlos Machado
lead_characters.demographics: Latino male, late teens/early 20s, Miami/Hialeah, family-bound, gun access, emotionally fragile.
lead_characters.hook: Carlos is the script's second tragic mirror, a young man whose despair is triggered by Jesse's public performance and the surrounding culture of violence. His family scenes give the movie a grounded emotional counterweight to the satire.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that can launch a young actor the way Lucas Hedges in Manchester by the Sea or Xolo Maridueña in Blue Beetle did: raw vulnerability with a late-film emotional payoff.

lead_characters.name: President Bowman
lead_characters.demographics: Male, mid-40s, President of the United States, charismatic, vulgar, politically powerful.
lead_characters.hook: President Bowman is a grotesque populist who treats Jesse's suicide spectacle as both entertainment and statecraft. He is outrageous, but the script makes him feel like a natural endpoint of the same attention economy Jesse is exploiting.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do full-throttle political satire in the mode of Bryan Cranston in Your Honor or Kelsey Grammer in Boss: swagger, threat, and absurdity.

lead_characters.name: Jeeves
lead_characters.demographics: Humanoid robot, British-accented voice, non-human performance requirement.
lead_characters.hook: Jeeves is the eerie, polite machine at the center of Mario's worldview, and its deadpan protocol makes the satire land harder. It is both comic relief and a symbol of the script's deepest anxiety about automation and obedience.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is motion-capture or voice-performance showcase territory in the vein of Andy Serkis's Gollum or Alan Tudyk's K-2SO: a non-human role with distinct personality and scene-stealing precision.

casting_characteristics: One lead with heavy dialogue and emotional volatility
Multiple 20s-40s supporting roles with specific age and status texture
Several roles with race/ethnicity specificity in the page text

notable_requirements: Manhattan condo, nightclub, strip club, corporate HQ, Harvard Club, karaoke bar, Palm Beach estate, Miami/Hialeah family home, beach and pool-party locations
Remote luxury estate and large ballroom sequence
Multiple city-specific settings across New York, Los Angeles, Palm Beach, and Miami

technical.vfx_details: News inserts, market graphics, livestream interfaces, helicopter coverage, crowd scale, and the humanoid robot Jeeves require compositing and interface work rather than heavy spectacle.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunfire, car crash, drowning sequence, overdose staging, blood effects, and practical destruction beats.

rights_flags.detail: "Is That All There Is?" by Peggy Lee

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: adult satirical thriller with awards-leaning commercial upside and strong streamer positioning.

budget.note: Contemporary production, but the script spans Manhattan, Los Angeles, Palm Beach, and Miami, with nightclub, estate, ballroom, helicopter, crowd, and stunt-heavy sequences that keep it above a contained indie footprint.

casting.note: Jesse needs a lead who can carry rapid-fire satire, humiliation, manic escalation, and emotional collapse; Mario, Brenda, Andrea, Mikey, and President Bowman all need actors with sharp comic timing and authority.

development.note: The script is built on a very specific satirical premise and a large number of named institutions, brands, and public-facing systems; the tonal balance between dark comedy, thriller escalation, and tragic ending is a major buyer conversation.

comp_set.title: The Social Network
comp_set.why_it_comps: Matches the tech-era anxiety, verbal velocity, and the sense that a single ambitious young man can become a cultural event.

comp_set.title: Nightcrawler
comp_set.why_it_comps: Like this script, it follows a morally elastic protagonist who monetizes catastrophe and keeps climbing as the world rewards him.

comp_set.title: Triangle of Sadness
comp_set.why_it_comps: Comps on satirical bite, class grotesque, and the way wealth and spectacle become the engine of the film.

comp_set.title: Don't Look Up

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who like sharp, topical satire about tech, money, and media collapse, especially viewers who respond to morally compromised antiheroes.
audience_target.demographics: 25-54, slightly male-skewing but viable with women who like prestige satire; educated urban/suburban audience, streamer-native, awards-aware.

budget_tier.note: Multiple city settings, luxury interiors, nightclub/estate/ballroom sequences, crowd work, practical stunts, and licensed music push this above a lean indie while staying below studio-scale spectacle.

types_of_buyers: streamer originals team building adult prestige genre
indie financier/distributor looking for awards-leaning commercial satire
lane_fit.detail: This sits in the lane where topicality, performance, and a high-concept hook can justify a mid-budget feature. The script has enough set-piece energy and social bite to attract buyers who want something smarter and stranger than a standard thriller.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the premise is built around one specific public countdown and one specific social-media/market event, not a reusable franchise engine.

strengths.what_it_means: This gives the project a clean commercial elevator pitch and a strong trailer promise, which is exactly what helps a buyer understand the movie in one pass. It will attract executives, actors, and directors who want a concept that feels current without needing explanation.
strengths.evidence: Jesse's layoff note, the suicide countdown, and the prediction market that prices his death at different odds.

strengths.what_it_means: The script isn't just making jokes about tech culture; it turns the satire into a thriller engine, which broadens the audience beyond pure comedy buyers. That makes it attractive to streamer dev teams and producers looking for elevated genre with topical bite.
strengths.evidence: The Harvard Club meltdown, the tour, the Nervy deal, and the Palm Beach climax all escalate the same premise in new forms.

strengths.dimension_or_area: A lead role built for a breakout performance
strengths.what_it_means: Jesse is the kind of part that can redefine an actor's lane because it requires speed, shame, charm, and volatility in constant collision. That is valuable to casting directors and managers because it can launch or reframe a career.
strengths.evidence: Jesse's oscillation between self-pity, manipulation, and genuine panic in the Harvard Club, the podcast speech, and the final livestream.

strengths.dimension_or_area: A triangle that keeps generating scenes
strengths.what_it_means: Jesse, Mikey, and Andrea create a durable relationship engine that can carry dialogue scenes, betrayals, and reversals without needing constant external plot. That is a real packaging advantage because it gives the movie emotional structure beyond the headline premise.
strengths.evidence: Their investment scheme, the wedding reveal, the hotel-room fallout, and the final breakup all come out of the same triangle.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Worlds that feel like separate pressure chambers
strengths.what_it_means: The script moves through tech, nightlife, finance, politics, and family life in a way that makes each setting feel like a different social system. That gives the project texture and makes it easier to market as a bigger cultural portrait rather than a single-location gimmick.
strengths.evidence: ShareStop HQ, the Harvard Club, Palm Beach, Hialeah, and the Miami family home all produce different kinds of conflict.

whats_special.headline: This is a sharp, high-concept satirical thriller with a lead role that can launch an actor and a premise that sells itself in one sentence. The script also has enough production texture and relationship engine to justify a mid-budget, prestige-leaning package for a streamer or specialty theatrical buyer.

items.area: The ending asks for a very specific tonal buy.
items.detail: The final movement goes from satire to blood-soaked political grotesque to near-mythic escape, and that is a real buyer conversation. If the audience is not already aligned with the script's heightened register, the last act can read as a hard tonal pivot rather than an inevitable escalation.

items.area: Jesse is concept-strong before he is fully human.
items.detail: The script gives him a brilliant engine, but much of his identity is expressed through behavior, rhetoric, and market logic rather than interiority. That is fine for a high-concept thriller, but it narrows the range of actors and makes the emotional landing more conditional on performance.

items.area: The music and brand stack needs real clearance work.
items.detail: "Perfect Day," "Is That All There Is?," and "Sail Away" are not decorative references; they are structurally important to the movie's emotional architecture. On top of that, the script leans heavily on named platforms and institutions like LinkedIn, Instagram, Facebook, Nervy, FutureDays, and ShareStop, which means business affairs will want a careful pass.

items.area: The production footprint is wider than the premise suggests.
items.detail: The movie moves from Manhattan to Los Angeles to Palm Beach to Miami, with clubs, estates, ballrooms, a helicopter, and crowd scenes. That is still manageable for a feature, but it is not a contained one-location buy, and the scope will matter in budget conversations.

items.area: The satire depends on a lot of named systems.
items.detail: ShareStop, Beings, Nervy, FutureDays, the President, the Pope, and the prediction-market apparatus all do heavy lifting in the premise. That density is part of the appeal, but it also means the script is less plug-and-play than a cleaner genre piece and will require a buyer comfortable with topical specificity.

issues.headline: The biggest friction is not the premise; it's the degree of tonal and packaging specificity the premise demands. This is a sharp, ambitious feature, but the buyer has to be comfortable with a very particular satirical register, a wide production footprint, and a lead role that lives or dies on the actor.
